property_summary: For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract returns true when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId and/or type(IAccessControl).interfaceId according to ERC165 semantics (specifically it always reports support for IERC165), whereas the mutant returns false for IERC165 (so there exists some interfaceId — namely IERC165's id — for which the reference returns true but the mutant returns false).

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference contract reports support for IERC165 when queried (supportsInterface returns true for type(IERC165).interfaceId), whereas the mutant fails to report IERC165 support (returns false for that id), so there exists an interfaceId — IERC165's — where reference returns true but mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct contract always reports support for IERC165 (supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) == true), while the mutant fails to report support for IERC165 (returns false for that specific interface id), so there exists an input (the IERC165 interface id) where the return differs.

For every bytes4 id, C.supportsInterface(id) returns true when id == type(IERC165).interfaceId (i.e. C always reports support for IERC165); the mutant violates this by returning false for that specific id, so there exists an interfaceId (IERC165's) where the return differs.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, calling c.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never reverts and in particular returns true when queried with the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId); the mutant flips IERC165 support and will return false for that specific id, so there exists an interfaceId (IERC165's id) where the return differs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true iff the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (or both via inheritance), while the mutant incorrectly returns true for the unrelated id 0xffffffff; thus for some fuzzed interfaceId (specifically 0xffffffff) the mutant reports support but the reference does not.

For any 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C.supportsInterface never claims support for the unrelated id 0xffffffff (i.e., returns false for that id unless other interfaces match), while the mutant incorrectly returns true for interfaceId == 0xffffffff; thus for all inputs the reference never returns true solely because of 0xffffffff, and the mutant does for at least that input.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface never returns true solely because the id equals 0xffffffff (it only returns true for IAccessControl or IERC165), while the mutant erroneously returns true for interfaceId == 0xffffffff, so there exists an input (0xffffffff) for which the mutant's return differs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface never returns true solely because the id equals 0xffffffff (it only returns true for IERC165 or IAccessControl), whereas the mutant incorrectly reports support for interfaceId == 0xffffffff, so there exists an interfaceId (0xffffffff) for which the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C.supportsInterface never claims support for the unrelated id 0xffffffff (i.e. returns false for that id unless it matches a true supported interface), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns true for interfaceId == 0xffffffff, so there exists an input (interfaceId == 0xffffffff) where the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For any interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true exactly when the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., for at least one known interfaceId it returns true), whereas the mutant always returns false and thus fails to report supported interfaces for those ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for at least the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) whereas the mutant always returns false, so the reference will report support for IERC165 but the mutant will not.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C's supportsInterface does not revert and returns either true for known interfaces (like IERC165 or IAccessControl) while the mutant always returns false; thus the general rule: there exists at least one interfaceId (fuzzed) for which reference returns true or false consistently with type checks — we assert that calling supportsInterface with any fuzzed id does not revert on the reference (ok==true), while the mutant may still not revert but will return false for at least some ids, so the reference always completes the call (no revert) for all ids whereas the mutant differs in return value for some ids — we detect this by fuzzing an interfaceId and asserting the call completes (no revert) on the reference.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface call never reverts (callable) and returns true when asked about IERC165's interfaceId; the mutant always returns false, so there exists an interfaceId (specifically type(IERC165).interfaceId) for which the reference returns true while the mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never reverts and in particular it returns true for IERC165's interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId), whereas the mutant always returns false and thus will return a different value for that specific interface id.

For any interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true iff the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., it only reports support for those known interfaces and not for arbitrary ids); the mutant that always returns true violates this by claiming support for other random ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) in the reference returns true only for the known supported interfaces (IERC165 or IAccessControl) whereas the mutant returns true for all interfaceIds; thus there exist interfaceIds for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface either returns true only for the known interfaces (IERC165 or IAccessControl) or false otherwise; the mutant reports true for all ids, so there exist ids where C returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns true for arbitrary ids beyond its supported interfaces (it returns true only for IERC165 or IAccessControl), whereas the mutant reports true for all interfaceIds; thus there exist interfaceIds where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface never returns true for arbitrary ids other than IERC165 or IAccessControl (it only returns true for those), whereas the mutant reports true for all ids — so there exist interfaceIds where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For any role and account, the reference contract returns true from hasRole iff the account is recorded as a member; the mutant inverts this return (so for some role/account the mutant's hasRole differs), hence the property that hasRole(role,account) == !hasRole_mutant(role,account) is violated by the mutant for some inputs (i.e. there exist role/account where reference returns true and mutant returns false and vice versa).

For any role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns whether the account is recorded as a member (true iff member); the mutant inverts this boolean, so there exist role/account pairs where hasRole differs — we assert that for any fuzzed role and account the reference's hasRole and the stored membership (via checking hasRole after granting and revoking) behave consistently, which the mutant will break for some inputs.

For any role and account, after granting the role to that account the contract's hasRole(role, account) must return true (and after revoking it must return false); the mutant that inverts the stored membership will produce the opposite result for some fuzzed inputs and thus violate this rule.

For any role and account, if the account is granted a role then hasRole(role, account) returns true (and after revocation returns false); the mutant that returns the inverse boolean will break this rule for some fuzzed role/account sequences.

For any role and account, if the contract grants that role to the account then hasRole(role, account) must return true (and after revoking it must return false); the mutant that inverts the stored membership will break this by returning the opposite boolean for some fuzzed role/account combinations.

For any role bytes32, the reference contract returns the stored admin role for that role (possibly different from DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE); the mutant instead always returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, so there exist roles where getRoleAdmin(role) != DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE which the mutant misreports.

For any role bytes32, the reference contract's getRoleAdmin(role) returns the admin role stored for that role (which may differ from DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE for some roles); the mutant always returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, so there exist roles where the returned value differs.

For every role r, the reference contract returns the stored admin role (which may differ from DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) via getRoleAdmin(r); the mutant always returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, so there exist roles r for which getRoleAdmin(r) != DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE and the mutant breaks this property.

For every role bytes32, the reference contract's getRoleAdmin(role) returns the stored admin role (which was set during construction or setup), whereas the mutant always returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE causing a mismatch for any role whose stored admin is not DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE.

For every role r the contract's getRoleAdmin(r) returns the actual stored admin role (as observable via granting rights: only accounts with that admin can grant the role); the mutant that always returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE will allow an account that is not the real admin to appear as admin and thus violate the property for some fuzzed role/account combinations.

For any role input, the reference contract returns the stored admin role (which may differ from the role itself); the mutant that returns the role itself violates this when a role's admin is not equal to the role (i.e., any role whose admin was set differently).
